p: It was on the fifteenth of October, seventeen sixty-four, as he sat musing amid the ruins of the Capitol in Rome, while the barefoot friars were singing vespers in the temple of Jupiter, that Mr Edward Gibbon first conceived the idea of writing the decline and fall of the city. So he tells us, in his memoirs, and so every historian since has repeated, with envy. Twelve years later the first volume appeared, and was on every table. The last appeared in seventeen eighty-eight. It is, as I have said, the greatest work of history in our language, and it would be presumptuous of me to retell in a few minutes what he told in six volumes. But every historian must face the question of why Rome fell, and here is my answer, such as it is.

In the second century after Christ, under a succession of able emperors whom Gibbon calls the five good emperors, the Roman Empire stretched from the north of Britain to the Euphrates, from the Rhine and the Danube to the Sahara. Gibbon thought it the period in the history of the world during which the condition of the human race was most happy and prosperous. That is a large claim, and I doubt that the slaves in the mines of Spain would have agreed with it. But it is true that some fifty or sixty million people lived under a single law, in peace, with roads, aqueducts, baths and theatres, for longer than any comparable population before or perhaps since.

In the third century the structure nearly collapsed. Between the years two hundred and thirty-five and two hundred and eighty-four there were more than twenty emperors recognised at Rome, nearly all of whom died violently, most at the hands of their own soldiers. Persian armies invaded from the east and Germanic peoples from the north. A terrible plague swept the empire. The coinage was debased until it was nearly worthless. The empire was saved, at enormous cost, by a series of hard soldier-emperors from the Balkans, and at last by Diocletian, who divided the government between several emperors, doubled the army, and taxed the people more heavily than ever before to pay for it. Constantine founded a new capital at Constantinople, on the Bosphorus, and the empire was thereafter divided, more and more permanently, into an eastern half governed from Constantinople and a western half governed, generally, not from Rome but from Milan or Ravenna, which were nearer the frontiers.

In three hundred and seventy-six, a people called the Goths, fleeing from the Huns, a terrible nomadic people from the steppes of Central Asia, crossed the Danube into the empire, with permission, as refugees. They were so ill-treated by the Roman officials, who sold them dogs for food in exchange for their children as slaves, that they rebelled, and in three hundred and seventy-eight they destroyed a Roman army at Adrianople and killed the emperor Valens. In four hundred and ten, the Goths under their king Alaric sacked the city of Rome itself, the first time in eight hundred years that a foreign enemy had entered it. Saint Jerome, in Bethlehem, wrote that the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken. Saint Augustine, in Africa, wrote his great book The City of God partly to answer those who blamed the disaster on the abandonment of the old gods.

In four hundred and six, a great confederation of Germanic peoples crossed the frozen Rhine. The western provinces fell away one by one: Britain was abandoned about four hundred and ten; Spain was overrun; the Vandals crossed into Africa and took Carthage in four hundred and thirty-nine, depriving the western government of its richest province and its grain. Attila the Hun ravaged Gaul and Italy in the years four hundred and fifty-one and four hundred and fifty-two, and died, in four hundred and fifty-three, of a burst blood vessel on his wedding night. The Vandals sacked Rome in four hundred and fifty-five, so thoroughly that their name has become our word for wanton destruction, which, the Encyclopaedia says, is rather unfair to them. And in four hundred and seventy-six, a Germanic general named Odoacer deposed the last emperor in the West, a boy named Romulus Augustulus, which means little Augustus, and sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, saying that one emperor was enough. It is the date in the textbooks. Nobody at the time thought it remarkable.

Gibbon's own answer was famous and, in its time, scandalous: he described the triumph of barbarism and religion, holding that Christianity had turned men's minds from the defence of the state to the salvation of their souls. Others have blamed lead in the water pipes, the decline of the birth rate, the exhaustion of the soil, the debasement of the coinage, the plague, the corruption of the court, the selfishness of the rich, the immensity of the frontiers. A German scholar of the twentieth century, the Encyclopaedia records, collected two hundred and ten explanations that have been proposed.

My own view, for what it is worth, is the view now most common among the scholars of the future. The western empire did not fall from some inner rot that had been decaying it for centuries; the eastern empire, which shared all the same vices, survived for another thousand years. It fell because it faced, at the same time, invasions too numerous to resist, civil wars that turned its armies against each other, and the loss of the tax revenue of its richest provinces, without which it could not pay the armies it needed. Each loss made the next more likely. It was a downward spiral, not a slow decay. The process took about eighty years.

Some scholars of the future prefer not to speak of a fall at all, but of a transformation: the Roman world slowly becoming the world of the Middle Ages, with Germanic kings ruling Roman provinces through Roman officials and the Latin church. There is truth in this. But the archaeologists remind us that in the century after the fall, the houses got smaller, the cattle got smaller, the pottery got coarser, the coins disappeared, and the population of the city of Rome fell from perhaps a million to a few tens of thousands. Whatever we call it, for those who lived through it, it was a catastrophe. Civilisation is more fragile than it looks from a comfortable study in Bath.
